extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / journalism reporters learning feature and interview writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing human-interest interviews, using background material, and composing personality sketches (feature/interview/biography hybrids) that reveal character and read vividly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage business reveals personality
rubrics_metrics.description: How is personality revealed through stage business? Is the setting suggested in harmony or in contrast with the person interviewed? List all the phrases that make the person seem alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete stage actions and small physical details (stage business) to show who the person is. Identify phrases that make the interviewee 'seem alive.' Contrast or harmony between setting and person can deepen characterization. (Exercise guidance: list stage-business phrases and underline references to the speaker.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting in harmony or contrast with subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the setting suggested in harmony or in contrast with the person interviewed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the setting supports or counters the subject's character; use that relation deliberately to illuminate personality. Early presentation of setting helps orient the reader to the occasion and gives context for character details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: What evidences of economy in writing do you find?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be concise; only include details that serve character, action, or necessary context. Exercises prompt reporters to identify economy in published interviews—short, precise phrasing and omission of irrelevant material are signs of good economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prewriting research for a personality sketch
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing: Interview the person. Gather anecdotes or other biographical material from friends and associates. Note what explains his success. Note what is unexpected or incongruous in tastes, character, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect primary material (the subject's own words) and corroborating anecdotes from associates. Focus on facts and anecdotes that explain achievements or reveal contrast/incongruity; these items become raw material for dramatization rather than commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask questions that elicit stage business and revealing detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate the questions you think the reporter put to the person interviewed to get the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design questions to draw out actions, anecdotes, habits, and sensory details (stage business) rather than abstract statements. Exercises recommend reconstructing the reporter's questions as a method to learn how to elicit revealing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine dramatic (conversation) and narrative styles
rubrics_metrics.description: To write the sketch: Use a combination dramatic (conversation) and narrative style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend quoted or reported dialogue with narrative sequencing and description. Follow directions for the human interest interview and the feature story; study model sketches and imitate effective mixes of scene and summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select highlights and use the dramatist's method
rubrics_metrics.description: The personality story may be wider in scope. High lights are selected and combined to make the person lifelike. The personality sketch is really characterization, and the method is the dramatist's method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to present a thumbnail portrait or to emphasize a single illuminating episode. Choose scenes and anecdotes that dramatize central traits; arrange them to create a coherent impression rather than attempting exhaustive biography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commentary; show rather than tell
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUTIONS: Don't comment. Show personality through 1. What the person does. 2. What others say of him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist authorial summarizing or moralizing. Let actions, stage business, quotations, and third-party anecdotes supply judgment and characterization. 'Don't comment' is an explicit anti-pattern to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a rich intellectual/background reservoir
rubrics_metrics.description: GOOD journalist must have a rich background. To acquire this background he should read a great deal—the classics, history, economics, literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely (classics, history, economics, literature) so you have standards and allusive material to draw upon. A broad background yields apt analogies and allusions that add color and resonance to reporting and headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw on classical, mythological, historical, or Biblical references judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Many a headline—or whole feature story—owes its lightness and grace, or its punch, to the cleverness of the writer in drawing upon literary, classic, mythological, historical, or Biblical sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use allusions to lend compact resonance and flavor (examples: 'Heel of Achilles,' Poe's raven references). Ensure references are apt and accessible to readers; they should enhance meaning rather than obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific, vivid headlines and lead lines that leverage background and characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A clever allusive headline or a vivid opening line can give a story lightness, grace, or punch and touch a responsive chord in the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft leads and headlines that compress character or irony using well-chosen allusions or vivid scene-setting. The text provides many model headlines and openings to study as exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice observation: record concrete local detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reporter, like the scientist, must be a keen observer. List the objects on your block that you would paint if you wanted to present a picture of your block. Do you know what gives your block its personality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train observational skills by cataloging tangible details in a scene. These small, concrete items (sound, smell, gestures, objects) are the building blocks of compelling stage business and vivid sketches.
